# Uniform response learning and stable composition in ferromagnetic environments

2026-11-04. Status: scoped mathematical construction; independent review is recorded separately in AUDIT.md. No priority, general-inference, or transformative-consequence claim.

## 1. Missing operation and precise scope

Ordinary TV accuracy of an isolated block does not control relative partition errors or its response after rare conditioning. Here we prove a stronger statement for a specific environment cone: nonnegative external weights with nonnegative Fourier coefficients. It includes arbitrary-strength ferromagnetic couplings, consistent nonnegative fields, and hard equality constraints. For product boundary fields we give a complete polynomial-time response learner and sampler from passive data. For general environments we prove a composition/error certificate, NOT an unconditional efficient contraction algorithm.

Let P=p_C be a distribution on k ordered spins, with all odd moments zero and all even moments Pf(C_S). Assume additionally that every even moment is nonnegative. These properties hold for free-boundary, zero-field ferromagnetic planar Ising networks, when the observed spins occur in cyclic order on a single face. The hidden bulk graph and its size need not be known.

We receive iid full-boundary samples from this ISOLATED zero-field distribution, not samples of the block embedded in an unknown environment. Correct ordering, equilibrium sampling, and the model promise are assumptions, not conclusions.

For any antisymmetric A define the signed mass
p_A(x)=2^(-k) sum_(S even) Pf(A_S) x_S,
where x_S=product_(i in S)x_i and Pf(empty)=1. It has total mass one. The empirical pair matrix A=C+Delta need not describe a physical model. Set D=sum_(i<j)|Delta_ij|.

An admitted environment weight W is a nonnegative function on the boundary with Fourier expansion
W(x)=sum_S w_S x_S, with every w_S>=0.
Assume Z=E_P W>0. W need not factor across sites and need not be planar.

## 2. Derivative identity

For a matching M of r disjoint index pairs, let U be its endpoints. Differentiating the Pfaffian expansion gives
partial_M p_C(x)=sigma_M 2^(-2r) x_U p_(C_(U complement))(chi x),
where sigma_M is the crossing sign of the selected pairs and chi_l=(-1)^(number of selected arcs whose interiors contain l). A mixed derivative whose selected pairs share an endpoint is zero.

Proof.

## Verdict

The weighted relative-error theorem, product-field response algorithm, rare same-sign conditioning claim, and joint multiblock stability certificate pass this independent review under their explicit promises. No blocking algebraic or runtime error was found. The crucial positivity is that of the true marginal and its true even moments, not of an empirical reconstructed law or an interpolating model. General-environment efficient contraction, model certification, physical sampling costs, novelty and practical advantage remain unproved.

This report independently checked the reasoning rather than treating the author's numerical tests as proof. Supplementary exact rational checks covered 433 weighted derivative and prefix cases through six spins, including deterministic-support true laws, signed reconstructions, hard pins, non-pairwise Fourier-positive weights, and coupled independent blocks. Tests are internal and are not part of a proof-only package.

## 1. The essential weighted step

For a matching M with endpoint set U, differentiating the Pfaffian Fourier polynomial leaves a uniform law on U times a spin-flipped true marginal on U's complement, with an overall signed spin monomial. Its absolute value is therefore a normalized nonnegative law, even for crossing matchings. A repeated endpoint gives a zero mixed derivative. The sign-flip rule counts selected arcs containing each unselected vertex; crossing signs among selected arcs contribute only an overall sign removed by the absolute value.

Averaging W over U eliminates every Fourier monomial meeting U. Its expectation under the residual spin-flipped marginal is the sum of w_S chi_S E_P x_S over S disjoint from U. True odd moments vanish. All other true moments and all stipulated w_S are nonnegative. Dropping chi_S signs and restoring omitted terms consequently bounds this expectation by Z=E_P W. There is no independence assumption on spins within a block and no division by a small assignment probability.

## Verdict

No counterexample or substantive mathematical error found in the stated theorem. The relative-error interface, finite-sample product-field response algorithm, sequential signed-mass repair, and multi-block certificate are justified under their explicit promises. This is not a general contraction algorithm and not a proof of novelty or practical superiority. The positivity assumptions, isolated-data contract, and distinction between signed algebra and sampled surrogates are essential.

## 1. Weighted derivative bound survives the rare-event attack

A mixed derivative with respect to disjoint upper-triangular pair coordinates has absolute value equal to a normalized product of: uniform spins on the removed endpoints, and a sign-flipped genuine marginal on the remaining coordinates. Its total mass is exactly one. Shared-endpoint derivatives vanish.

For nonnegative W with nonnegative Fourier coefficients, its expectation in this derivative law is

sum over S avoiding removed endpoints of w_S chi_S m_S.

Odd moments vanish; even m_S are nonnegative. This expression is at most sum_S w_S m_S = Z, by removing sign flips and restoring omitted nonnegative terms. The left side is nonnegative because both W and the absolute derivative law are nonnegative. No lower bound on a particular assignment probability is used.

Taylor expansion is around the genuine C only. Every surviving monomial is a matching, hence the weighted absolute error is bounded by Z times the sum of products of absolute coordinate perturbations. Bounding this sum by exp(D)-1 is valid. No positivity of any interpolated matrix, Taylor intermediate, or reconstructed distribution is required.

The same-sign rare-event example is sound: for H of size r, W=product_{i in H}(1+x_i), Z=2^r P(all H are plus), and Z>=1 because its Fourier constant is one and all contributing moments are nonnegative. Thus P(event)>=2^-r. The known factor 2^-r introduces the exponentially small probability without an ill-conditioned normalization. Relative error in Z is exactly relative error in the event probability. This does not extend to a mixed-sign assignment.
